title: AgenticVBench: Can AI Agents Complete Real-World Video Production Tasks?
claim: The benchmark consists of several distinct task families, each defined by a clear input-to-agent-to-output specification covering a different part of the workflow.
layout: 2x2 grid of panels, each Input → Agent → Output, colored headers
description: A 2x2 grid presents the four task families of the benchmark. Each quadrant has a colored title pill (1 Assembly in salmon, 2 Repair in green, 3 Sequencing in blue, 4 Repurpose in yellow) and a short gray subtitle. Inside each quadrant, an Input box on the left connects through a robot-icon Agent and an arrow to an Output box on the right. Assembly shows candidate shots plus a requirement document, producing a video built from Slot 1…N. Repair shows a defective film strip with a red box, a list of defect types, and a repaired strip with a green box and a checklist. Sequencing shows shuffled sketch clips that become an ordered grid, with order strings below. Repurpose shows an 11-minute source video plus requirements, producing a 1-minute recap built from selected key frames. Film-strip frames and cinematic stills dominate the visual weight.
caption: Overview of the four task families in AgenticVBench. Assembly evaluates storyboard-aligned shot selection and video construction, Repair focuses on defect localization and correction, Sequencing tests causal and temporal shot ordering, and Repurpose measures long video condensation into short-form deliverables such as recap, trailer, teaser, and social cut.
abstract: Video production workflows offer a rich and demanding arena for evaluating multimodal AI agents: they require composite capabilities across text, image, audio, and video understanding, along with long-horizon planning, and tool use. To this end, we introduce AgenticVBench, a benchmark of 100 agentic tasks across 4 task families spanning the real world post-production workflow, constructed from real production workflows contributed by 20 industry experts averaging 6 years of professional experience. Tasks are paired with evaluation specifications that combine programmatic verifiers and expert rubrics. We evaluate frontier vision-language models (VLMs) with both vendor-native and open-source harnesses. The best evaluated agent stack barely crosses 30%, far below human expert performance on the same tasks. We further find that the choice of harness substantially affects model behavior, including scores, tool-use patterns, and failure modes. AgenticVBench provides a foundation for diagnosing and improving both models and harnesses for agentic video production. Benchmark website: https://agenticvbench.com.
